Title: Instruction-Evidence Contrastive Dual-Stream Decoding for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning

Instruction-Evidence Contrastive Dual-Stream
Decoding for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning

Abstract
Vision–Language Models (VLMs) exhibit strong performance in instruction follow-
ing and open-ended vision-language reasoning, yet they frequently generate fluent
outputs that are weakly grounded in visual evidence. Prior works have shown that
instruction prompting further worsens this issue by amplifying language priors, es-
pecially when the visual signal is uncertain or ambiguous. To address this challenge,
we propose a decoding framework that explicitly balances linguistic informative-
ness and visual faithfulness during generation. Our method, Instruction-Evidence
Contrastive Dual-Stream Decoding (IECD2), maintains two parallel probability
distribution of tokens at each decoding step: an instruction-driven stream that
promotes expressive and informative responses, and an evidence-driven stream that
enforces strict grounding in the image. These two streams are adaptively fused
using a symmetric KL-based contrastive gate, which suppresses tokens favored
by language priors but unsupported by visual evidence, while preserving them
when both distributions agree. We evaluate IECD2 on multiple datasets spanning
various generative vision-language reasoning tasks such as captioning and visual
question answering on multiple datasets such as, POPE, MME, VQAv2, AMBER,
MS-COCO, and LlaVA-Bench. IECD2 demonstrates consistent improvements
in task accuracy and reasoning performance, alongside a substantial reduction in
hallucination across all evaluation metrics compared to state-of-the-art decoding
approaches.
1
Introduction
To enable unified multimodal interpretation and generation, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in-
tegrate large language models (LLMs) with pretrained visual encoders. Despite their impressive
capabilities, VLMs remain prone to hallucination, producing fluent and plausible descriptions or
answers that are not supported by the image. Prior work attributes this behavior to dataset bias and
the dominance of language priors when visual evidence is weak or ambiguous (You et al. [2024],
Zhu et al. [2021], Zhibo et al. [2023]). To tackle this, Contrastive Decoding (CD) (Li et al. [2023a])
offers a training-free alternative by explicitly contrasting token distributions under different contexts,
suppressing tokens driven by spurious or biased language priors while retaining those supported by
reliable visual evidence. In this work, building on the notion of instruction disturbance introduced in

Instruction Contrastive Decoding (ICD) (Wang et al. [2024b]), which appends role-based prefixes
to modulate multimodal alignment uncertainty in VLMs, we further examine how variations in
instruction prompt influence the internal token distributions and contribute to visually inconsistent
generation.
Empirically, instruction-aligned prompts induce a distribution that favors informativeness and cover-
age, whereas prompts that explicitly constrain the model to rely only on visible evidence strongly
suppress hallucination but often lead to overly conservative and less descriptive outputs (Liu et al.
[2024b]). This reveals a fundamental trade-off between linguistic richness and visual faithfulness:
prompt formulations do not merely control surface style, but actively shift the probability mass toward
either language-prior-dominated or evidence-grounded decoding regimes.
Motivated by this observation, we propose that instruction-following and evidence-grounding prompts
produce complementary but contradictory token distributions. Rather than committing to either mode,
we preserve both distributions and reconcile them dynamically during generation. As illustrated in
Fig. 1, this leads to our Instruction–Evidence Contrastive Dual-Stream Decoding (IECD2), which
maintains parallel instruction and evidence streams—capturing language priors and strict visual
grounding, respectively—and adaptively fuses them at each decoding step through a divergence-
aware contrastive gate. By explicitly contrasting linguistic priors against visual grounding, IECD2
suppresses hallucination when the two disagree, while retaining fluency and descriptive power when
they align. Our contributions are as follows:
1. We propose IECD2, a dual-stream decoding framework that explicitly maintains paral-
lel instruction-driven and evidence-grounded token distributions throughout generation,
enabling decoding to jointly model linguistic priors and visual grounding.
2. We introduce a divergence-based contrastive gating mechanism that resolves conflicts
between instruction and evidence streams. By measuring bidirectional disagreement via
symmetric KL divergence, the gate selectively suppresses hallucination-prone tokens while
preserving informative language content.

3. We conduct extensive experiments on vision-language reasoning tasks such as captioning
and VQA and IECD2 consistently reduces hallucination and improves grounding accuracy
while maintaining descriptive coverage.

Related Work
Hallucination in VLMs refers to the generation of fluent but visually unsupported content, including
nonexistent objects, incorrect attributes, or fabricated relations (Liu et al. [2024a], Bai et al. [2025]).
Earlier work in NLP characterized hallucination as a factual inconsistency with source inputs (Maynez
et al. [2020]), while in vision-language settings, object hallucination has emerged as a central concern
(Rohrbach et al. [2018]). Hallucinations in VLMs are categorized into three types: category, attribute,
and relation (Bai et al. [2025]). However, most existing methods are designed to improve overall
visual grounding and factual consistency by mitigating multiple hallucination types simultaneously.
Category Hallucination.
Category-level hallucination arises when a model predicts the presence of
an object class that is not supported by the image, often driven by strong language priors and dataset
frequency bias. Inference-time correction methods aim to mitigate this effect without retraining.
Post-hoc verification frameworks such as Woodpecker (Yin et al. [2024]) revise generated outputs
using auxiliary detectors or external consistency checks; however, such pipelines depend on addi-
tional models and handcrafted decision rules, introducing error propagation and limiting scalability to
open-ended generation. Contrastive decoding (Li et al. [2023a]) offers a training-free alternative by
explicitly contrasting token distributions induced by clean and disturbed inputs, where the disturbance
refers to perturbations that weaken visual grounding (e.g., corrupted images or misleading instruc-
tions). Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) (Leng et al. [2024]) suppresses category hallucination
by contrasting predictions from original and visually perturbed images, thereby down-weighting
object tokens that remain confident under visual corruption and are thus likely language-prior driven,
while Instruction Contrastive Decoding (ICD) (Wang et al. [2024b]) exploits disturbance in the
instruction space to expose category-level hallucinations amplified by prompt-induced language bias.
Multi-Frequency Contrastive Decoding (MFCD) (Liu et al. [2025]) introduces frequency-domain
disturbances by selectively removing high- and low-frequency components from images to isolate
hallucination-prone distributions. Object-aligned visual contrastive decoding (Chen et al. [2026])
masks salient object regions to produce semantically meaningful counterfactual inputs that enhance
visual grounding and suppress language-driven object predictions.
Attribute Hallucination.
Attribute hallucination occurs when a model assigns incorrect properties
(e.g., color, size, state) to visually present objects. VACoDe (Kim et al. [2024]) addresses this by
selecting among multiple image augmentations to maximize contrast, encouraging the model to
discount attribute predictions that are unstable under visual variation. Re-Balancing Contrastive
Decoding (RBD) (Liang et al. [2024]) further targets attribute errors by correcting imbalanced cross-
modal attention, reweighting textual and visual contributions to prevent over-dominance of language
priors in attribute realization. From an internal representation perspective, IFCD (Wang et al. [2025a])
contrasts disturbed hidden states to suppress spurious attribute logits, while VaLiD (Wang et al.
[2025b]) introduces uncertainty-aware layer-wise fusion to counteract attribute distortions caused by
noisy visual encoding.
Relation Hallucination.
Relation hallucination refers to incorrect spatial or semantic relationships
between objects (e.g., left-right, holding, riding), which often emerge from long-range dependency
errors and misaligned multimodal reasoning. Token-level and adaptive strategies such as CATCH
(Kan et al. [2024]) dynamically gate contrastive strength at each decoding step, allowing the model to
suppress relation tokens when visual support is weak. Octopus (Suo et al. [2025]) further observes that
hallucination types vary across decoding stages and proposes a multi-strategy contrastive framework
that adaptively switches among disturbance sources to correct relation-level inconsistencies. Extend-
ing contrastive decoding to multi-source reasoning, Multi-Path Information Contrastive Decoding
(MPI-CD) (Ruan et al. [2025]) introduces a tri-branch framework that contrasts predictions from
original, salient-region, and non-salient-region inputs to enhance multimodal reasoning and reduce
hallucinations arising from incorrect relational associations.

3
Methodology
In this section, we introduce Instruction-Evidence Contrastive Dual-Stream Decoding (IECD2), a
training-free decoding framework for mitigating object hallucinations in VLMs. IECD2 maintains two
token-probability streams during generation: an instruction-guided stream and a visually grounded
evidence stream. These streams are fused using a divergence-aware gating mechanism that suppresses
instruction-only predictions when they diverge from visual evidence to reduce overdependence on
language prior and improve grounded generation. Section 3.1 formalizes the dual-stream formulation,
while Section 3.2 presents the divergence-aware fusion mechanism.
3.1
Dual-Stream Token Distributions
Prior work has shown that hallucinations in VLMs are often amplified by instructional prompting,
which encourages models to prioritize response fluency and task completion over strict visual
grounding. To explicitly separate these two behavioral tendencies, IECD2 maintains two parallel
decoding streams throughout generation, both instantiated from the same underlying VLM but
conditioned via different prompt contexts, shown in Figure 1. Formally, at each decoding step t given
history y<t, we construct two token probability distributions, Instruction stream and Evidence stream,
over the shared vocabulary space.

Behavior.
The gating mechanism exhibits the following behavior:
• Small divergence (Dt ≈0): The two streams agree closely, indicating that the instruction-
driven continuation is already consistent with visible content. In this case, gt remains
moderate, allowing the instruction stream to retain stronger influence, thereby preserving
linguistic fluency and descriptive richness.
• Large divergence (Dt ≫0): The instruction stream may diverge from the evidence stream
when the model relies excessively on language priors, such as predicting commonly expected
objects that are not actually present in the image. In such situations, gt decreases sharply
toward 0, reducing the contribution of the instruction stream and encouraging the decoder to
rely more on visually grounded evidence for token generation.
Evidence Stream alone is not fully reliable because, while it is strictly grounded in visible cues and
avoids hallucination, it is overly conservative and tends to under-emphasize higher-level semantic
concepts such as actions and interactions. As illustrated in the Fig. 2, it assigns low probability to
activities like playing or running despite their plausibility, since it focuses on local visual attributes
rather than integrating broader contextual and relational information. Consequently, its predictions
5


can be incomplete or overly literal, motivating the need to combine it with the instruction stream in
IECD2 to achieve both visual accuracy and semantic completeness.
Unlike static weighting strategies (Li et al. [2023a], Leng et al. [2024], Wang et al. [2024b]),
contrastive gating enables IECD2 to operate adaptively. IECD2 preserves descriptive expressiveness
when the model is visually consistent while actively constraining object speculation only when
hallucination risk is detected.
4
Experiments
4.1
Experimental Settings
Benchmarks.
We evaluate IECD2 across five widely-used VLM datasets. POPE (Li et al. [2023b])
benchmark isolates object hallucination by asking binary object-existence queries under adversarial,
popular, and random sampling conditions. MME (Fu et al. [2025]) benchmark measures multimodal
perception and cognition, including existence recognition, attribute reasoning, counting, OCR,
landmark identification, translation and commonsense inference. General visual question answering
ability is assessed on the VQAv2 (Goyal et al. [2017]) validation split, which consists of open-ended
answer type questions. Hallucination in caption generation is evaluated on Caption Hallucination
Assessment with Image Relevance (CHAIR) (Rohrbach et al. [2018]) on the MSCOCO validation
set (Lin et al. [2014]). Following prior work, we randomly sample 500 images from the validation
split and generate captions for evaluation and we perform this experiment 5 times and report the
average performance. Finally, we use the AMBER (Wang et al. [2024a]) benchmark to evaluate
grounding robustness on a generative captioning task and a discriminative verification task. Together,
these datasets jointly assess hallucination suppression, visual grounding reliability, and task-level
vision-language reasoning capability. LLaVA-Bench (Liu et al. [2023]) comprises of 24 images
accompanied by 60 queries that encompass a variety of contexts, including indoor and outdoor scenes,
memes, paintings, and sketches. This dataset is designed to evaluate the ability of VLMs to address
more complex tasks and their adaptability to novel domains. We perform a qualitative analysis of this
dataset to illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed IECD2.
Evaluation Metrics.
For POPE, we report standard binary-classification metrics: Accuracy and F1
score. For MME, we follow the official leaderboard protocol and report normalized aggregate score
(Accuracy+). For AMBER, we evaluate the generative task using CHAIR, together with Coverage,
Hal, and Cog to quantify grounding reliability, and compute Accuracy and F1 for the discriminative
verification task. For VQAv2, we report the standard VQA accuracy, while hallucination robustness
is further assessed via CHAIR metrics, CHAIRi and CHAIRs, computed on MS-COCO val2014
captions. On POPE and MME, we measure grounding reliability under binary verification and
perception tasks. On VQAv2, MS-COCO captioning, and AMBER, instruction-aligned VLMs are
known to be more prone to visually unsupported generation (Liu et al. [2024b]).
VLMs used.
We evaluate IECD2 on two representative vision–language models, LLaVA-1.5-7B
(Liu et al. [2023]) and InstructBLIP (Dai et al. [2023]) (Vicuna-7B backbone) that are also used
by other decoding approaches. These VLMs differ in visual encoders, multimodal alignment, and
instruction-tuning strategies, providing a diverse testbed for evaluating hallucination mitigation. For
all VLMs across datasets, IECD2 is applied only at decoding time without parameter updates or
retraining, enabling a fair and model-agnostic evaluation.
Implementation Details.
For each model, we compare its default decoding with IECD2 using
instruction and evidence prompts from Section 3, setting instruction temperature TI = 1.0, evidence
temperature TE = 0.9, and η = −3.0, with symmetric KL divergence for contrastive gating. The
instruction and evidence temperatures control the sharpness of the token distributions generated by
each stream. A lower temperature produces a sharper distribution, assigning higher probability to a
few top-ranked tokens and making the stream more confident in its predictions. In contrast, a higher
temperature produces a flatter distribution, distributing probability more evenly across multiple tokens
and reducing prediction confidence. Decoding lengths are limited to 3–16 tokens for VQA and 20–64
tokens for captioning, and all experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA L40 48GB GPU.

4.2
Ablation Studies
4.2.1
Effect of Dual-Stream Design
To verify that IECD2 dual-stream formulation is essential rather than incidental, we conduct an
ablation study on the MSCOCO Captioning task using LLaVA-1.5-7B. We compare IECD2 with
Instruction stream only, which uses the standard instruction-aligned generation and Evidence stream
only, which enforces strict visual grounding. Quantitative results in terms of CHAIRs and CHAIRi
are reported in Table 1. Instruction stream only baseline exhibits the highest hallucination, indicating
a strong tendency to introduce plausible but unsupported objects under purely instruction-driven
decoding. Evidence stream only variant substantially reduces hallucination by enforcing strict visual
grounding, but this rigid constraint often leads to conservative and less expressive captions. In
contrast, IECD2 achieves the lowest hallucination rates, outperforming both single-stream variants.
These results confirm that hallucination mitigation is not achieved merely by suppressing language
priors, but by explicitly contrasting instruction-driven and evidence-grounded token distributions.
The KL-gated fusion in IECD2 adaptively down-weighs hallucination-prone probability mass while
retaining the descriptive richness of instruction-aligned generation, providing a more effective and
balanced decoding strategy.

4.2.2
Effect of Temperature and Contrastive Gating Strength η
To analyze the sensitivity of IECD2 to decoding hyperparameters, we perform ablations on the
AMBER Generative Task using LLaVA-1.5-7B by independently varying the instruction temperature
TI, the evidence temperature TE, and the contrastive gating strength η, and report CHAIR, Coverage,
Hallucination rate (Hal), and Cognitive Hallucination (Cog) in Table 2. We observe that stronger
contrastive gating (i.e., more negative η) consistently reduces hallucination, as reflected by decreasing
CHAIR and Hal, while Coverage remains largely stable, indicating that the KL-guided gate sup-
presses unsupported content without sacrificing descriptive quality; similarly, lowering the instruction
temperature yields slightly more conservative yet stable captions, increasing it promotes richer
language at a marginal cost to Coverage, and reducing the evidence temperature sharpens visually
grounded token probabilities and further mitigates hallucination, with overall trends demonstrating
that IECD2 remains stable across a wide range of hyperparameters and does not rely on fragile tuning
for effective and robust deployment.

4.2.3
Ablation Study on the MME Benchmark
We analyze the behavior of IECD2 on a benchmark that consists of diverse perception and cognition
tasks covering multiple types of hallucinations, to study how the instruction and evidence streams
contribute to visual understanding. As shown in Table 3, on the perception tasks, IECD2 achieves
strong performance on core object-level categories, including Existence (190.0 for both LLaVA-1.5
7


and InstructBLIP), Counting (165.0 and 55.0), and Color recognition (160.0 and 115.0). Performance
on spatial and contextual categories is also stable, as observed for Position (116.67 for LLaVA-1.5
and 48.33 for InstructBLIP) and Scene understanding (162.25 and 163.50). These results indicate
that relying solely on language priors or solely on visual cues is insufficient, and that hallucinations
arising from either source can be effectively mitigated when both streams are jointly considered.
The contrastive gating mechanism combines the strengths of the two streams and resolves conflicts
between instruction guidance and visual evidence, leading to consistent performance across different
perception categories and backbone models. On the cognition tasks, IECD2 also shows stable
behavior, achieving 112.86 and 77.50 on commonsense and code reasoning for LLaVA-1.5, and
104.29 and 65.00 for InstructBLIP, respectively, further demonstrating that the interaction between
instruction and evidence is essential for robust performance on hallucination-sensitive evaluation
settings.

4.3
Experimental Results
4.3.1
Results on VQA
We evaluate IECD2 on three representative discriminative benchmarks, namely POPE (MSCOCO),
MME, and AMBER Discriminative Task, which collectively assess visual grounding reliability and
object-attribute reasoning under diverse bias conditions.
POPE (MSCOCO).
POPE explicitly probes object-level hallucination under Random, Popular,
and Adversarial sampling regimes. As shown in Table 5, IECD2 yields clear improvements over
standard decoding for both LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP. Averaged across the three settings, IECD2
improves Accuracy by up to 4.9% and 5.1%, with corresponding F1 gains of 5.0% and 4.8%,
respectively. Moreover, while strong baselines such as ICD, VCD, VaLiD, IFCD, CATCH, and
Octopus exhibit notable performance drops when moving from Random to Adversarial splits, IECD2
shows a smaller degradation margin (approximately 4-6%), indicating improved robustness against
frequency-induced bias and adversarial object confusions.
AMBER Discriminative Task.
The AMBER Discriminative Task measures discriminative visual
grounding. As reported in Table 5, IECD2 consistently improves grounding accuracy across different
VLMs. On LLaVA-1.5, IECD2 achieves an Accuracy/F1 of 77.8/82.6, corresponding to relative gains
of +12.4% and +14.7% over direct decoding (69.2/72.0). Similarly, on InstructBLIP, IECD2 attains

We evaluate IECD2 on three representative captioning benchmarks-MSCOCO Captioning and AM-
BER Generative Task, to assess its impact on open-ended visual reasoning and hallucination suppres-
sion.
MSCOCO Captioning.
To quantify object-level hallucination in caption generation, we report
CHAIRs and CHAIRi on a randomly sampled subset of 500 MSCOCO validation images. As
shown in Table 6, for LLaVA-1.5, IECD2 achieves CHAIRs/CHAIRi scores of 2.96/2.25, compared
to 20.0/15.2 under direct decoding, corresponding to absolute reductions of 85.2% and 85.1%,
respectively. Relative to strong baselines such as IFCD (13.2/5.6) and CATCH (14.3/4.7), IECD2
further reduces CHAIRs by 77.6% and 79.3%, and CHAIRi by 59.8% and 52.1%. For InstructBLIP,
IECD2 attains 0.60/0.78, improving over direct decoding (48.0/13.9) with reductions of 98.8% in
CHAIRs and 94.4% in CHAIRi, and also outperforming ICD, VCD, and IFCD by large margins.
These results demonstrate that IECD2 provides the strongest suppression of hallucinated object
mentions among all compared decoding strategies.
AMBER Generative Task.
On the AMBER benchmark, which explicitly measures hallucination
severity and coverage, IECD2 yields substantial reductions in hallucination-related metrics. As shown
in Table 6, for LLaVA-1.5, IECD2 achieves CHAIR/Hal/Cog scores of 2.3/5.6/0.4, compared to
9.2/44.5/31.0 under direct decoding. This corresponds to absolute reductions of 75.0% in CHAIR,
87.4% in Hal, and 98.7% in Cog. For InstructBLIP, CHAIR is reduced from 8.4 to 3.8 (54.8%
reduction) and Cog from 2.6 to 0.5 (80.8% reduction). While strong methods such as Octopus
also achieve notable suppression, IECD2 attains comparable or better generative grounding while
simultaneously improving discriminative performance and requiring no retraining. Overall, the
AMBER results confirm that divergence-aware dual-stream decoding effectively constrains open-
ended generation toward visually supported content, leading to more stable and reliable captions.
Inference Time.
IECD2 exhibits distinct runtime behavior across tasks and caching settings.
Without KV cache, it requires 2.378 seconds per query for generative tasks and 0.129 seconds
for discriminative tasks. The average number of generated tokens per query is 38.31. With KV
cache enabled, the generative inference time decreases substantially to 1.144 seconds, whereas the
discriminative setting shows a moderate increase to 0.167 seconds. At the token level, KV caching
reduces the per-token cost for generative queries (from 0.066s to 0.032s), while introducing a slight
overhead for discriminative queries (from 0.065s to 0.080s). This trend reflects the effectiveness of
caching in autoregressive generation, where repeated reuse of past key-value states improves effi-
ciency, in contrast to discriminative settings where shorter sequences limit reuse and introduce cache
management overhead. A detailed breakdown of per-stream and per-token costs is provided in Table 7.

Qualitative Analysis
To analyze the qualitative behavior of IECD2, we visualize captioning results on the LLaVA-Bench
(Liu et al. [2023]) dataset, as shown in Fig. 3, and compare IECD2 with IFCD (Wang et al. [2025a])
to highlight differences in visual grounding and reliance on language priors.
In the first example, IFCD speculates about the person’s identity and the dog’s emotions, while
IECD2 simply describes a stylized image of a man lifting a small dog against a cloudy sky. In the
second example, IFCD infers intent and urgency from a handwritten webpage sketch, whereas IECD2
reports only the visible layout and text elements. In the third example, IFCD hallucinates specific
meat types in a sandwich image, while IECD2 limits itself to visible ingredients and the “Subway
Series” logo. In the fourth example, IFCD assigns emotions and specific food categories to illustrated
animals, whereas IECD2 describes three animals seated around a tree-stump table with food items. In
10


the final example, IECD2 lists the visible contents of a refrigerator shelf, while IFCD gives only a
vague summary. Overall, IECD2 produces short, accurate, and visually grounded captions, avoiding
identity speculation and unsupported semantic inferences that frequently appear in IFCD outputs.
5
Conclusion
We presented Instruction–Evidence Contrastive Dual-Stream Decoding (IECD2), a decoding-time
framework that improves the reliability of vision–language model generation by explicitly contrasting
instruction-driven and evidence-grounded token distributions. By maintaining two parallel proba-
bility streams and fusing them through a symmetric KL–based adaptive gate, IECD2 dynamically
suppresses visually unsupported continuations while preserving linguistic fluency when the two
distributions are consistent. This formulation enables the model to balance language priors and visual
grounding at each decoding step, rather than committing to a single prompting regime. Extensive
experiments across both generative and discriminative vision–language reasoning tasks show that
IECD2 consistently reduces hallucination and improves grounding accuracy, demonstrating that
contrastive, divergence-aware fusion at inference time is an effective and general mechanism for
enhancing the robustness of modern VLM decoding.

Abstract: Vision–Language Models (VLMs) exhibit strong performance in instruction follow- ing and open-ended vision-language reasoning, yet they frequently generate fluent outputs that are weakly grounded in visual evidence. Prior works have shown that instruction prompting further worsens this issue by amplifying language priors, es- pecially when the visual signal is uncertain or ambiguous. To address this challenge, we propose a decoding framework that explicitly balances linguistic informative- ness and visual faithfulness during generation. Our method, Instruction-Evidence Contrastive Dual-Stream Decoding (IECD2), maintains two parallel probability distribution of tokens at each decoding step: an instruction-driven stream that promotes expressive and informative responses, and an evidence-driven stream that enforces strict grounding in the image. These two streams are adaptively fused using a symmetric KL-based contrastive gate, which suppresses tokens favored by language priors but unsupported by visual evidence, while preserving them when both distributions agree. We evaluate IECD2 on multiple datasets spanning various generative vision-language reasoning tasks such as captioning and visual question answering on multiple datasets such as, POPE, MME, VQAv2, AMBER, MS-COCO, and LlaVA-Bench. IECD2 demonstrates consistent improvements in task accuracy and reasoning performance, alongside a substantial reduction in hallucination across all evaluation metrics compared to state-of-the-art decoding approaches.
